title: Elara and the Dragon's Warning
markdown:
Elara Vance reached Aethelgard’s gates with a rogue shoelace and a flurry of misplaced notes. Ancient Dragon Linguistics waited, her worst subject, the one her prodigious memory for odd facts refused to help. She could recite the 1,472 scales on a shadow-viper’s tail and the napping spots of moon-moths. Draconic conjugations slid off her like rain. The downpour had already slicked the village stones until the lane looked awake. She was still late.

“Elara. Dear.” Paloma Crumble, her neighbour, stood under a bright red umbrella with a wicker basket. “A bit damp. Mrs Higgins’s ginger snaps. Fortifying. And a jam tart that would forgive a clock.”

Ten minutes late, dread knotting, Elara took the warmth. Professor Abernathy’s stare would be ice. Her brain, sharp on cloud-fish migration and giggle-berry circumference, still fumbled tenses.

The academy grounds hummed wrong, anxious as a late bell. Tiny dragons, usually a riot of emerald and sapphire flitting the enclosures, huddled. Their chirps were distressed squeaks, not happy trills. Elder Herder Maeve wrung her hands, serenity gone, usually as reliable as sunrise. “Never this restless. Not even in the dew-drop shortage. Their scales are duller.”

Elara, still tasting ginger, tried to keep her eyes on the Draconic Lament of the First Sigh and failed. The calls had a staccato she knew from a footnote she had filed and forgotten on purpose, the way she forgot shoelaces. Paloma offered another snap without comment, which was a neighbour’s finest dialect.

The pattern rose. Not a lament. A dialect the tome named Whispers of the Shifting Sky, page 477, the page she had skipped because it would not conjugate.

“Paloma,” she said, tight. “That dialect. I remember it.”

Paloma polished a damp pocket watch, dry as a biscuit. “Does it mention more jam tarts?”

Elara’s memory, the fickle friend, yielded. The textbooks would call it a localised atmospheric disruption, Abernathy’s favourite gravitas. The chirps said something sharper: a shimmering cascade of airborne instability, rare, the sort that thinned enchantments. The wards that kept Aethelgard and its charges steady would flicker. Senior herders had heard noise. Elara, trapped in the subject she outran, heard a forecast.

“It isn’t only the dragons,” she said, startling a gardener into dropping his can. “The wards. They’ll flicker. We reinforce them now.”

Headmaster Thorne’s white beard held more secrets than the restricted section. He looked at her the way a dragon looks at a coin. Paloma offered slightly-too-crumbly shortbread as carb-based diplomacy. Elara traced chirp to syllable until the picture was too clear to file under anxiety.

The sky went iridescent, a kaleidoscope that stole breath. Shimmering air washed the hillside. Stones hummed. The wards pulsed, then steadied: hurried reinforcements, her warning’s only useful homework. The tiny dragons quieted. Sheen returned to their scales, a shy polish. Below, the village came out of the downpour and seemed to exhale as the colours receded.

They walked home under the folded red umbrella. Paloma did not ask for a conjugation. Elara ate the last ginger snap and did not apologise for the time. The lane shone. The dragons, behind them, sounded like themselves again, small and ordinary and enough.
characters: Elara Vance (bright but chronically late scholarship pupil who has a sharp memory for odd details), Paloma Crumble (a neighbour who brings snacks to every crisis)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, fantastic story for curious young teens
author: StoryGen Community
